panels.title: Status — is it running, and is it sending?
Mode
panels.description: The single most important fact about a running instance. 1 means every transaction is built, signed and then logged; 0 means it is on the wire.

panels.title: Replication
panels.description: While this is 0 the worker learns about nothing new. Stream positions are stale.

panels.title: Synapse DB access
panels.description: A shadow must be read-only. A primary sender must NOT be — its cursor is a set of deletions.

panels.title: Destinations known
panels.description: Queues that exist. Grows to this worker's share of the destination list and stops.

panels.title: Backing off
panels.description: Destinations refusing to be dialled. A large number is NORMAL — a homeserver's destination list is mostly a graveyard. Watch its SHAPE: a step change means a problem at our end, not theirs.

panels.title: Version
panels.description: Build stamped at compile time.

panels.title: Throughput — this worker against Synapse's own senders
Events examined per second
panels.description: Examined counts every event the pickup loop looked at; routed counts those that produced at least one destination in this shard. Most events are remote-origin and are correctly skipped, so the gap between the two lines is expected and large.

panels.title: Transactions per second
panels.description: Not directly comparable while shadowing: this worker covers ONE shard and the Synapse line covers every sender. Compare the shapes, not the heights.

panels.title: Events skipped, by reason
panels.description: Shape matters more than height. 'remote origin' dominating is correct — most traffic is other servers' events. A filter that suddenly rejects everything shows up here as a change in composition, not merely a drop in throughput.

panels.title: Event processing lag (p50 / p95 / p99)
panels.description:
THE comparison. Both are seconds from the event being persisted to routing finishing. Note Synapse also exports synapse_event_processing_lag, which is a millisecond gauge and NOT the same measurement.

Only meaningful while FOLLOWING the stream. During a replay every event is hours old by construction and this says nothing about speed — read the stage panel instead.

panels.title: Where the time goes, per stage (p95)
panels.description:
The panel that says WHERE to optimise, and it has already answered once: the goroutine fan-out this design bets on costs microseconds, while destination resolution costs milliseconds. The bottleneck is the database, not the concurrency model.

Unaffected by replay, unlike the lag panel.

panels.title: Fan-out duration (p50 / p95 / p99)
panels.description: Time to hand one event to every destination queue in this shard. The number the whole design is a bet on.

panels.title: Destinations per routed event
panels.description: The fan-out width — how many servers one event has to reach. This is the cost Synapse pays on a single reactor and the reason this worker exists.

panels.title: Queued work
panels.description: Sampled rather than tracked by counter, so a leak shows up even when the counters that should have caught it are themselves the buggy part. Steady growth means delivery is not keeping up with routing.

panels.title: Send duration by outcome (p95)
panels.description: Labelled by outcome because a fast failure and a fast success are indistinguishable in a duration histogram — a remote that refuses instantly would otherwise read as excellent performance.

panels.title: Sends in flight
panels.description: Against queue.max_concurrent_destinations. Pinned at the bound means the concurrency limit, not the network, is what is pacing delivery.

panels.title: Replication rows by stream
panels.description: A stream that stops arriving is invisible everywhere else: the worker simply has less to do and looks healthy.

panels.title: Stream position lag behind Synapse
panels.description: Two senders walking the same stream. A widening gap is this worker falling behind.

panels.title: Shadow record — read this before promoting
Approximate routes, by cause
panels.description:
Routing decisions that fell back to CURRENT room state instead of resolving the state before the event, which is what Synapse does.

'forked dag' is work not done here — full state resolution is room-version-specific and expensive. 'prev event has no state group' is an outlier nobody could have resolved. The two mean different things and only the first is addressable.

panels.title: Persisted shadow totals (survive restarts)
panels.description: Restored from disk at startup, so these are cumulative across deploys. The promotion gate is measured in weeks and cannot be judged from counters that reset.

panels.title: Shadow record age
panels.description: How long the persisted totals have been accumulating. The promotion question is 'has this agreed for weeks', so this is the denominator.

panels.title: Restarts since record began
panels.description: A suspiciously good match rate should be checked against how long the worker has actually been up.

panels.title: Primary mode — bookkeeping written to Synapse's tables
Write operations per second
panels.description:
Always zero in shadow mode, and that is worth being able to see: a shadow that started writing would be changing the real senders' behaviour.

In primary mode, a sender's cursor IS these deletions.

panels.title: Write failures
panels.description: Non-zero here in primary mode means delivery is working while the bookkeeping is not: rows are re-read forever, the outbox grows without bound, and prev_id chaining silently lags. Nothing else reports it.
